territorial_scope.description: Applies as a chapter of Washington state law (Title 42 RCW) to electioneering communications concerning candidates for elective office.

evidence.quote: BE IT ENACTED BY THE LEGISLATURE OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON:

summary.short: Creates a civil remedy for candidates whose appearance, speech or conduct is altered by synthetic media in an electioneering communication: injunctions and damages against the sponsor, with limited liability for media, and a disclosure-based affirmative defense. Directs the Public Disclosure Commission to adopt rules.
summary.long: The act adds a new chapter to Title 42 RCW. Synthetic media is an intentionally manipulated image, audio or video recording of an individual, made with generative adversarial network or other digital technology, that is realistic but false and gives a fundamentally different impression than the original. A candidate whose appearance, action or speech is altered by synthetic media in an electioneering communication may seek injunctive or equitable relief against its publication, or general or special damages against the sponsor, and a prevailing party may recover reasonable attorneys' fees and costs. The plaintiff must prove use of synthetic media by clear and convincing evidence. It is an affirmative defense that the communication carries a disclosure that the media has been manipulated, placed as prescribed for visual or audio media. Sponsors may be held liable; a medium is liable only if it removes the disclosure or changes content to create synthetic media, and federally licensed broadcasters subject to 47 U.S.C. 315 are excluded. Interactive computer service providers and users are not treated as publishers of third-party information, subject to the same exception. The public disclosure commission must adopt rules; the chapter does not create a violation under chapter 42.17A RCW or authorize commission action under RCW 42.17A.755. The text states no effective date.

relations.target_text: chapter 42.17A RCW (Revised Code of Washington, campaign finance chapter)
relations.note: Sec. 1 imports the definitions used in chapter 42.17A RCW into this chapter. The target is not in the registry, so target_instrument_id is empty.

evidence.quote: The definitions used in chapter 42.17A RCW apply throughout this chapter

relations.note: Sec. 4 states that the act does not authorize the public disclosure commission to take action under RCW 42.17A.755, a section of chapter 42.17A.

evidence.quote: authorizes the public disclosure commission to take action under RCW 42.17A.755

relations.note: Sec. 3(2) excludes from the medium-liability rule electioneering communications by a licensee, programmer or operator of a federally licensed broadcasting station that are subject to 47 U.S.C. Sec. 315.

evidence.quote: Except when a licensee, programmer, or operator of a federally licensed broadcasting station transmits an electioneering communication that is subject to 47 U.S.C. Sec. 315

notes: Registry metadata gives RCW 42.62 as the chapter number, but the document only says a new chapter is added to Title 42 RCW (Sec. 5), so the number is not in the text. Sec. 2 uses 'electioneering communication' without defining it in this act; Sec. 1 imports chapter 42.17A definitions, which are not in the document. Sec. 2(1) joins clauses (a) and (b) with 'and', so both conditions apply. Sec. 4 says nothing in the chapter is a violation under chapter 42.17A. The text contains a stray line number '35' inside Sec. 6.

thresholds.value_text: if the audio is greater than two minutes in length
thresholds.measurement: Length of the audio recording in which the synthetic media disclosure is made; the text does not specify the measurement method.
thresholds.consequence: Where the audio exceeds two minutes, the disclosure must also be interspersed within the audio at intervals of not more than two minutes each.
thresholds.conditions: Applies only where the media consists of audio only and the affirmative-defense disclosure under Sec. 2(4)(b) is used.

evidence.quote: if the audio is greater than two minutes in length

events.note: No dated or datable event is stated in the text. It gives no adoption, signature, publication, entry-into-force or application date, and no phase-in, deadline, sunset, expiry or repeal date. Its only legislative marker is the enacting clause in the preamble ('BE IT ENACTED BY THE LEGISLATURE OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON:'), which carries no date. Section 4 directs the public disclosure commission to adopt rules but sets no deadline, and section 2(6) says courts are 'encouraged to determine matters under this section expediently' without a time limit.
